The roof coverings appear to have been replaced or re-covered at some point in the past and are now of interlocking concrete tiles which are considerably heavier than traditional clay or slate tiles. Internally, shakes and additional strutting supports have been provided, suggesting the roof has experienced some minor movement in the past. Your legal adviser should confirm whether Building Regulations approval was obtained for these alterations (see more comments in Sections E1 and H1).

The underfelt at the edges of the roof on the two-storey rear addition is not correctly lapped into the gutter. The primary function of roofing underfelt is to provide an additional layer of protection against water penetration. Properly lapping the felt into the rainwater gutter ensures that any water that gets beneath the roof tiles is directed into the gutter, preventing it from running down the fascia or into the building structure. If the roofing felt is not properly lapped into the gutter, water could potentially seep behind the gutter or into the wall structure, leading to dampness, rot, or other moisture-related issues. The underfelt should extend beyond the edge of the roof and into the gutter to ensure that water flows directly into the gutter. Further investigation by a competent roofing contractor is recommended to carry out the necessary repairs and ensure the roof coverings are fully watertight. Additionally, the condition of the roof timbers at the edges of the roof should be checked to ensure there is no rot.

The roof is of butterfly construction. These roof structures are utilised with horizontal valley gutters, which help run off of the rainwater. We could not inspect this section, as there was no available vantage point. Butterfly roofs are always potential problem areas and should be regularly inspected and repaired as necessary.

The rear verge to the roof is cracked and there is evidence of some cracking and loosening of the verge mortar and roof tiles at the edges. This could pose a health and safety risk if verge mortar falls, and immediate repairs are required. A reputable roofing contractor should be consulted, and quotations be obtained for any necessary repairs.

Moss and lichen growth was noted on the roof. There is some moss and lichen growth on the roof, which should be removed periodically. Moss and lichen can inhibit the roof’s efficiency by trapping moisture, which can lead to the deterioration of roof materials over time.

Roof lights have been installed. It is crucial to ensure that the flashing detail surrounding these roof lights is in good condition, as any failure could allow dampness to enter the property, leading to significant deterioration of the roof timbers. Generally, approval under the Building Regulations is required for the installation of a new roof light. Whilst our understanding is that the installation of roof lights typically does not necessitate planning permission, it is essential for your legal advisor to confirm this understanding (see Section H1).

Solar panels are installed on the roof. It should be confirmed by your legal adviser the Photovoltaic panels fitted to this property are wholly owned by the vendor or are leased under a lender approved scheme. We have not inspected or tested the panels and you should arrange for an inspection by a specialist. It is our understanding that installation of solar panels is generally considered to be permitted development. Your legal advisor should confirm our understanding (see Section I1).

History of underpinning. There is a history of underpinning to the property. It should be noted that different lenders may have different policies and approaches towards properties with history of underpinning. Your legal adviser should investigate and request the relevant documentation for the works that have been undertaken and ensure all remedial work is carried out under a long term and meaningful guarantee with a suitable insurance indemnity. It is imperative that the relevant documentation for this is requested to include Building Regulations approval.

RAAC presence not ascertained. We could not ascertain whether the building contains reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC). As we are not specialists and have not undertaken any intrusive investigations or specialist tests, we cannot rule out the possibility that this material may be present. Your solicitor should make further enquiries with the building management as to whether any RAAC has been detected or if there is any information they may hold in their records, including any action plans, in regard to this matter. If RAAC has been or is identified, this is likely to have a large impact on the future saleability of the property and more importantly on the health and safety of the occupiers of the building. Whilst this is a worst-case scenario, these are the risks you should be aware of prior to purchase.

No hazardous material noted. No deleterious or hazardous materials were noted during the inspection.

Lintel defect. The small beam that spans across the top of the front bay opening (called a lintel) has a defect, and signs of cracking were noted to the window lintels in various locations, particularly evident at the lintel to the front bay. At this stage, the size of the cracks in the lintels does not justify significant structural intervention, and it is proposed to repair, repoint, and monitor them. The broken bricks can be replaced or resin grouted with low viscosity grout such as ‘Nitokit LV’ by Fosroc. If further movement is noticed after repairs are undertaken, the lintels will need to be either replaced or strengthened (by providing a steel plate to the underside of the masonry or similar). Replacement of the lintel will require Building Regulations approval.

Masonry bees. Masonry bees were noted. There are holes in the external walls, typical of those produced by masonry bees, which can cause substantial erosion and weakness of the joints. In severe cases this can affect the stability of the walling. The situation should be checked during the summer period when the bees are active and if these are seen entering the wall structure, the advice of the Environmental Health Officer of the Local Authority should be sought.

Crack to the front bay—Helifix bars and resin injection. The mortar joints at the abutment of the front bay and the main wall have cracked, and a gap was also noted to the left side of the bay. These cracks have appeared since apparent fairly recent repointing works were carried out, indicating that progressive movements are occurring. Therefore, we recommend to increase the tensile strength of the masonry fabric by installing stainless steel HeliFix bars between the bay structure and the main building walls to ensure that the abutment connection is strengthened and potential future movement is arrested. Regarding the repair of the cracks (which may be subject to further minor movement), it is standard practice to recommend that the external wall cracks are reinforced with the installation of Helifix bars and resin injection repairs. This involves inserting 6 mm diameter stainless steel bars into the bed joints at approximately 500 mm intervals on each side of the crack. The cracks in the bricks can either be replaced or resin grouted with a low viscosity grout such as Nitokit LV by Fosroc. The bars should be inserted every 2–3 courses of brick. A well-installed Helifix bar repair should blend into the façade and not be visibly prominent.

Crack to the front bay—repair to the lintel. In addition to the above crack repairs, the lintels to the front bay require repair, repointing and monitoring to address the defects and cracks noted.
